newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Rain gives some relief to parched Philippine farms.
newsitem.headline: Rain gives some relief to parched Philippine farms.

text.p: Sporadic monsoon rains are likely to benefit parched rice and corn farms in the Philippines but a drought is still expected later in the year, the Philippine weather bureau said on Tuesday.

The bureau's senior weather specialist Nathaniel Cruz said torrential rains which brought Manila to a virtual standstill on Tuesday were regular monsoon rains which lash the archipelago between April and September each year.
"It is flooded in Metro Manila, but most parts of the Philippines have been receiving sparse rains," Cruz said in an interview with Reuters.
"Rice and corn plants in the vegetative stage will benefit from the rains," Cruz said.
He still forecast a drought, however.
"Our forecast remains. We expect a drought because of El Nino starting in the fourth quarter," he added.
El Nino is caused by the warming of water in the western Pacific ocean, which creates disparate phenomena such as drought in some areas and heavier-than-usual rainfall in others.

Earlier this month, farmers in the Cagayan Valley and Bicol regions in the main Luzon island and South Cotabato in southern Mindanao island suffered planting delays and asked the government to conduct cloud seeding in their areas.
Philippine Sugar Regulatory chief Wilson Gamboa said local sugar crops would weather an expected arid stretch due to El Nino.
"The planting season for crop year 1997/98 will not be affected by the El Nino since the drought will be peaking late this year up to next year," he told reporters.
"By the time the El Nino event worsens, the sugar plants are already three feet high and no longer need much water."
